facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina could grow up to 8 meters long and weigh approximately 5000 kilograms.
facts.quote: Measuring up to 8 m in length and weighing around 5000 kg, Cretoxyrhina was one of the largest sharks of its time.

facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina possessed razor-like teeth up to 8 centimeters long with thick enamel designed for stabbing and slicing.
facts.quote: Its teeth, up to 8 cm long, were razor-like and had thick enamel built for stabbing and slicing prey.

facts.statement: Hydrodynamic calculations suggest Cretoxyrhina could reach burst speeds of up to 70 kilometers per hour.
facts.quote: Cretoxyrhina was also among the fastest-swimming sharks, with hydrodynamic calculations suggesting burst speeds of up to 70 km/h.

facts.statement: Researchers speculate that Cretoxyrhina hunted by lunging at prey at high speeds using strong eyesight, similar to modern great white sharks.
facts.quote: It has been speculated that Cretoxyrhina hunted by lunging at its prey at high speeds to inflict powerful blows, similar to the great white shark today, and relied on strong eyesight to do so.

facts.statement: Anatomical analysis suggests Cretoxyrhina possessed facial and optical features similar to thresher and crocodile sharks and likely used regional endothermy.
facts.quote: Anatomical analysis of the Cretoxyrhina skeletons revealed that the shark possessed facial and optical features most similar to that in thresher sharks and crocodile sharks and had a hydrodynamic build that suggested the use of regional endothermy.

facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina preferred subtropical to temperate pelagic waters but may have lived in water as cold as 5 degrees Celsius.
facts.quote: It preferred mainly subtropical to temperate pelagic environments but may have occurred in waters as cold as 5 C.

facts.statement: Charles H. Sternberg discovered the first well-preserved skeleton of Cretoxyrhina in 1890 and described it in a 1907 paper.
facts.quote: Charles H. Sternberg discovered the first skeleton in 1890, which he described in a 1907 paper:

facts.statement: While traditionally placed in the family Cretoxyrhinidae, some researchers have proposed classifying Cretoxyrhina within the families Alopiidae or Lamnidae.
facts.quote: Cretoxyrhina is traditionally classified as the likely sole member of the family Cretoxyrhinidae but other taxonomic placements have been proposed, such as within the Alopiidae and Lamnidae.

facts.statement: It is debated whether competition with the giant mosasaur Tylosaurus contributed to the extinction of Cretoxyrhina.
facts.quote: One factor in this demise may have been increasing pressure from competition with predators that arose around the same time, most notably the giant mosasaur Tylosaurus.

facts.statement: Charles R. Eastman published an analysis of a Cretoxyrhina skeleton in 1894.
facts.quote: Charles R. Eastman published his analysis of the skeleton in 1894.

facts.statement: A Cretoxyrhina skeleton sold by Sternberg to LMU Munich was destroyed in 1944 by Allied bombing during World War II.
facts.quote: This skeleton, which Sternberg had sold to LMU Munich, was destroyed in 1944 by allied bombing during World War II.

facts.statement: George F. Sternberg discovered a second O. mantelli skeleton in 1891, which is now housed in the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History as KUVP 247.
facts.quote: In 1891, Sternberg's son George F. Sternberg discovered a second O. mantelli skeleton now housed in the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History as KUVP 247.

facts.statement: George F. Sternberg found notable skeletons FHSM VP-323 in 1950 and FHSM VP-2187 in 1965.
facts.quote: His most notable finds were FHSM VP-323 and FHSM VP-2187, found in 1950 and 1965 respectively.

facts.statement: The skeleton discovered by Tim Basgall is housed in the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History as KUVP 69102.
facts.quote: This fossil is housed in the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History as KUVP 69102.

facts.statement: In 1958, Leonid Glickman proposed the new genus Cretoxyrhina based on the dental design of O. mantelli.
facts.quote: In 1958, Soviet paleontologist Leonid Glickman found that the dental design of O. mantelli reconstructed by Eastman made it distinct enough to warrant a new genus—Cretoxyrhina.

facts.statement: Leonid Glickman identified a second species, C. denticulata, based on earlier Cretoxyrhina teeth.
facts.quote: He also identified a second species of Cretoxyrhina based on some of the earlier Cretoxyrhina teeth, which he named C. denticulata.

facts.statement: Glickman's 1964 replacement of C. mantelli as the type species with 'Isurus denticulatus' is now rejected as an invalid taxonomic amendment.
facts.quote: Originally, Glickman designated C. mantelli as the type species, but he abruptly replaced the position with another taxon identified as 'Isurus denticulatus' without explanation in a 1964 paper, a move now rejected as an invalid taxonomic amendment.

facts.statement: Viktor Zhelezko erroneously invalidated the genus Cretoxyrhina in 2000 by synonymizing it with 'Pseudoisurus tomosus'.
facts.quote: This nevertheless led Russian paleontologist Viktor Zhelezko to erroneously invalidate the genus Cretoxyrhina in a 2000 paper by synonymizing 'Isurus denticulatus' (and thus the genus Cretoxyrhina as a whole) with another taxon identified as 'Pseudoisurus tomosus.

facts.statement: A 2013 study by Mikael Siverson reinstated the genus Cretoxyrhina and moved P. vraconensis into it.
facts.quote: A 2013 study led by Western Australian Museum curator and paleontologist Mikael Siverson corrected the taxonomic error, reinstating the genus Cretoxyrhina and moving 'P'. vraconensis into it.

facts.statement: In 2010, Charlie Underwood and Stephen Cumbaa described Telodontaspis agassizensis from teeth previously identified as juvenile Cretoxyrhina.
facts.quote: In 2010, British and Canadian paleontologists Charlie Underwood and Stephen Cumbaa described Telodontaspis agassizensis from teeth found in Lake Agassiz in Manitoba that were previously identified as juvenile Cretoxyrhina teeth.

facts.statement: A 2013 study by Michael Newbrey reaffirmed Telodontaspis agassizensis into the genus Cretoxyrhina using fossil material from Western Australia.
facts.quote: This species was reaffirmed into the genus Cretoxyrhina by a 2013 study led by American paleontologist Michael Newbrey using additional fossil material of the same species found in Western Australia.

facts.statement: The name Cretoxyrhina is a portmanteau of 'creto' (Cretaceous) and 'Oxyrhina', derived from Ancient Greek words meaning 'sharp' and 'nose'.
facts.quote: Etymology Cretoxyrhina is a portmanteau of the word creto (short for Cretaceous) prefixed to the genus Oxyrhina, which is derived from the Ancient Greek ὀξύς (oxús, "sharp") and ῥίς (rhís, "nose").

facts.statement: The common name 'Ginsu shark' was coined in 1999 by Mike Everhart and Kenshu Shimada, referencing the knife's 'slicing and dicing' action compared to C. mantelli's feeding mechanism.
facts.quote: The common name Ginsu shark, originally coined in 1999 by paleontologists Mike Everhart and Kenshu Shimada, is a reference to the Ginsu knife, as the theoretical feeding mechanisms of C. mantelli was often compared with the "slicing and dicing" when one uses the knife.

facts.statement: Between 1997 and 2008, Kenshu Shimada analyzed C. mantelli skeletons using modernized techniques to research the possible biology of Cretoxyrhina.
facts.quote: Between 1997 and 2008, Japanese paleontologist Kenshu Shimada published a series of papers where he analyzed the skeletons of C. mantelli including those found by the Sternbergs using modernized techniques to extensively research the possible biology of Cretoxyrhina.

facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina is traditionally classified within the family Cretoxyrhinidae, which belongs to the lamnoid sharks.
facts.quote: Cretoxyrhina has been traditionally grouped within the Cretoxyrhinidae, a family of lamnoid sharks

facts.statement: The earliest fossils of Cretoxyrhina date back to approximately 107 million years ago.
facts.quote: The earliest fossils of Cretoxyrhina are dated about 107 million years old

facts.statement: The youngest confirmed fossil of C. mantelli dates to 73.2 million years ago and was found in the Bearpaw Formation of Alberta.
facts.quote: The youngest fossil of C. mantelli was found in the Bearpaw Formation of Alberta, dating as 73.2 million years old

facts.statement: Some researchers suggest Cretoxyrhina may have survived into the Maastrichtian based on a tooth dated to 70.44 million years old, though this is debated due to the deposit being brackish water.
facts.quote: A single tooth identified as Cretoxyrhina sp. was recovered from the nearby Horseshoe Canyon Formation and dated as 70.44 million years old, suggesting that Cretoxyrhina may have survived into the Maastrichtian

facts.statement: A 2005 study by Shimada suggested Cretoxyrhina might be related to modern thresher sharks, but the study noted the results were premature and possibly inaccurate.
facts.quote: Phylogenetic studies through morphological data conducted by Shimada in 2005 suggested that Cretoxyrhina may alternatively be congeneric with the genus of the modern thresher sharks

facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina teeth are characterized by a triangular shape, razor-like non-serrated edges, visible tooth necks, and a thick enamel coating.
facts.quote: Distinguishing characteristics of Cretoxyrhina teeth include a nearly symmetrical or slanted triangular shape, razor-like and non-serrated cutting edges, visible tooth necks (bourlette), and a thick enamel coating

facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina had mackerel shark-like dentition with closely spaced tooth rows that did not overlap.
facts.quote: The dentition of Cretoxyrhina possesses the basic dental characteristics of a mackerel shark, with tooth rows closely spaced without any overlap

facts.statement: C. mantelli teeth averaged 3–4 cm in slant height, with the largest known specimen reaching up to 8 cm.
facts.quote: C. mantelli teeth are larger, measuring 3–4 cm in average slant height. The largest tooth discovered from this species may have measured up to 8 cm

facts.statement: Fossil skeletons such as FHSM VP-2187 provide a near-complete articulated dentition for C. mantelli, making its teeth among the best-known of all extinct sharks.
facts.quote: The dentition of C. mantelli is among the best-known of all extinct sharks, thanks to fossil skeletons like FHSM VP-2187, which consists of a near-complete articulated dentition.

facts.statement: Shimada reconstructed and later revised the dental formula for C. mantelli using fossil specimens in 1997 and 2002.
facts.quote: Using these specimens, the dental formula was reconstructed by Shimada (1997) and revised by Shimada (2002), it was .

facts.statement: C. mantelli likely used a "slicing and dicing" feeding mechanism similar to modern mako sharks, using spear-like front teeth to anchor prey and curved rear teeth to cut it.
facts.quote: The structure of the tooth row shows a dental structure suited for a feeding behavior similar to modern mako sharks, having large spear-like anteriors to stab and anchor prey and curved lateroposteriors to cut it to bite-size pieces, a mechanism often informally described as "slicing and dicing" by paleontologists.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that differences in tooth size and lateral profiles between C. mantelli individuals might represent sexual dimorphism or individual variations.
facts.quote: They discovered that two of these reconstructions show some notable differences in the size of the first intermediate (I1) tooth and lateral profiles, concluding that these differences could possibly represent sexual dimorphism or individual variations.

facts.statement: The rostrum of C. mantelli did not extend far forward from the braincase, suggesting it had a blunt snout.
facts.quote: The rostrum does not extend much forward from the frontal margin of the braincase, suggesting that the snout was blunt.

facts.statement: The elongated hyomandibula of C. mantelli was believed to swing laterally, allowing for jaw protrusion and deep biting.
facts.quote: The hyomandibula is elongated and was believed to swing laterally, which would allow jaw protrusion and deep biting.

facts.statement: Most species of the genus Cretoxyrhina are known only from fossil teeth and vertebrae.
facts.quote: Most species of Cretoxyrhina are represented only by fossil teeth and vertebra.

facts.statement: Fossils of C. mantelli from the Niobrara Formation are exceptionally preserved because the chalk contains high calcium levels that promote calcification.
facts.quote: Fossils of C. mantelli from the Niobrara Formation have been found exceptionally preserved; this was due to the formation's chalk having high contents of calcium, allowing calcification to become more prevalent.

facts.statement: The largest vertebrae of C. mantelli measured up to 87 mm in diameter.
facts.quote: The largest vertebra were measured up to 87 mm in diameter.

facts.statement: Specimens FHSM VP-2187 and KUVP 69102 have 218 and 201 vertebrae respectively, with nearly all vertebrae preserved except for portions of the tail tips.
facts.quote: Two specimens with the best-preserved vertebral columns (FHSM VP-2187 and KUVP 69102) have 218 and 201 centra, respectively, and nearly all vertebra in the column preserved; only portions of the tail tip are missing for both.

facts.statement: C. mantelli is estimated to have had approximately 230 vertebrae, a count unique among extant mackerel sharks which have either fewer than 197 or more than 282.
facts.quote: Estimations of tail length calculates a total vertebral count of approximately 230 centra, which is unique as all known extant mackerel sharks possess a vertebral count of either less than 197 or greater than 282 with none in between.

facts.statement: Large, circular vertebrae in the trunk region gave C. mantelli a spindle-shaped body with a stocky trunk.
facts.quote: The vertebral centra in the trunk region were large and circular, creating an overall spindle-shaped body with a stocky trunk.

facts.statement: The tail vertebrae of C. mantelli numbered between 70 and 90, making up approximately 30% to 39% of the total vertebral column.
facts.quote: The transition to tail vertebrae is estimated to be between the 140th and 160th vertebrae out of the total 230, resulting in a total tail vertebral count of 70–90 and making up approximately 30–39% of the vertebral column.

facts.statement: The transition from precaudal to tail vertebrae in C. mantelli featured a 45° bend, the highest angle known in extant sharks and typical of fast-swimming species.
facts.quote: The transition from precaudal (the set of vertebrae before the tail vertebrae) to tail vertebrae is also marked by a vertebral bend of about 45°, which is the highest possible angle known in extant sharks and is mostly found in fast-swimming sharks, such as lamnids.

facts.statement: Features including a lunate tail, smooth scales, a plesodic pectoral fin, and a spindle-shaped build indicate C. mantelli was capable of fast swimming.
facts.quote: These properties of the tail, along with other features such as smooth scales parallel to the body axis, a plesodic pectoral fin (a pectoral fin in which cartilage extends throughout, giving it a more secure structure that helps decrease drag), and a spindle-shaped stocky build, show that C. mantelli was capable of fast swimming.

facts.statement: C. mantelli possessed regional endothermy (mesothermy), featuring red muscles near the body axis and a rete mirabile system to conserve metabolic heat, similar to modern thresher and lamnid sharks.
facts.quote: Possessing regional endothermy (also known as mesothermy), it may have possessed a build similar to modern regionally endothermic sharks like members of the thresher shark and lamnid families, where red muscles are closer to the body axis compared to ectothermic sharks (whose red muscles are closer to the body circumference), and a system of specialized blood vessels called rete mirabile (Latin for "wonderful nets") is present, allowing metabolic heat to be conserved and exchanged to vital organs.

facts.statement: The partially warm-blooded nature of C. mantelli allowed it to function efficiently in the colder environments where its fossils have been found.
facts.quote: This morphological build allows the shark to be partially warm-blooded, and thus efficiently function in the colder environments where Cretoxyrhina has been found.

facts.statement: It is hypothesized that regional endothermy in Cretoxyrhina evolved in response to global cooling and competition from other endothermic marine reptiles like mosasaurs.
facts.quote: Regional endothermy in Cretoxyrhina may have been developed in response to increasing pressure from progressive global cooling and competition from mosasaurs and other marine reptiles that had also developed endothermy.

facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina had dense overlapping placoid scales with U-shaped grooves averaging 45 micrometers in width.
facts.quote: Cretoxyrhina possessed highly dense overlapping placoid scales parallel to the body axis and patterned in parallel kneels separated by U-shaped grooves, each groove having a mean width of about 45 micrometers.

facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina possessed a "Type 4" tail fin with a Cobb's angle of 49 degrees and a tail cartilage angle of 133 degrees.
facts.quote: Cretoxyrhina also had the most extreme case of a "Type 4" tail fin, having the highest known Cobb's angle (curvature of tail vertebrae) and tail cartilage angle (49° and 133° respectively) ever recorded in mackerel sharks.

facts.statement: Researchers infer that Cretoxyrhina was ovoviviparous, similar to modern mackerel sharks, despite a lack of fossil evidence.
facts.quote: Although no fossil evidence for it has been found, it is inferred that Cretoxyrhina was ovoviviparous as all modern mackerel sharks are.

facts.statement: A 2019 study found that an older C. mantelli individual died at approximately 26 years of age.
facts.quote: A 2019 study led by Italian scientist Jacopo Amalfitano briefly measured the vertebrae from two C. mantelli fossils and found that the older individual died at around 26 years of age.

facts.statement: A 2013 study identified a syntype tooth from England suggesting a C. mantelli maximum length of 8 meters.
facts.quote: The 2013 study also identified a syntype tooth of C. mantelli from England and calculated the individual's maximum length of 8 m, making the tooth the largest known specimen yet.

facts.statement: Species C. denticulata and C. vraconensis reached a maximum adult length of 4 meters.
facts.quote: C. denticulata and C. vraconensis reached a total body length of up to 4 m as an adult.

facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina occupied a top trophic level shared only with large mosasaurs like Tylosaurus in the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: The highest trophic level it occupied was a position shared only with large mosasaurs such as Tylosaurus during the latter stages of the Late Cretaceous.
